passage:
In Class 10 geography, Sharma Sir wrote that the Tropic of Cancer passes through Kerala. Disha's hand shot up. 'Sir, that's wrong! It goes through Madhya Pradesh. It's in our textbook!'
The class went 'Ooooh.' Sir's ears turned red. 'Sit down. Don't teach me my subject.'
At break Disha fumed to Pema. 'Why can't we correct them when they're wrong? It's just facts.'
Pema shrugged. 'You're right about the map. But you said it like a quiz-show buzzer.'
After the last bell Disha went to the staffroom, textbook open. 'Sir, I think page 42 says otherwise. Could you check?'
Sir looked, sighed, and nodded. The next morning he corrected the board himself.

qa.q: Where did Disha go after the last bell?
qa.a: To the staffroom, with the textbook open.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling at break while talking to Pema?
qa.a: Disha felt frustrated and wronged, sure of the facts and unable to see why a student cannot correct a teacher.

qa.q: What changed when Disha spoke to Sir in the staffroom?
qa.a: Disha spoke privately and politely and asked Sir to check page 42, so he could accept the correction without losing face.

qa.q: How might Sharma Sir have felt when the class went 'Ooooh'?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and challenged in front of everyone, which made him defensive even though the correction was right.

grounding: Shows a teenager honestly asking why a younger person cannot correct an elder who is wrong, and finding that a polite private correction is heard where a public challenge was not.

passage:
Dear Omkar Kaka,
I'm sorry about Sunday dinner. When you said Swara was wasting her life studying painting, I shouldn't have banged the table and said, 'You don't know anything about art.' That came out rude, and in front of everyone.
But I still want to ask you something honestly. Why is it wrong for someone younger to say an elder is mistaken? Swara won a state prize last year, and art graduates do find work. I think you were wrong about that, and I think I'm allowed to say so.
Can we talk about it on your next visit, just the two of us, over chai? I'll listen too. I promise not to bang anything.
Your nephew,
Ojas

qa.q: What did Ojas say at Sunday dinner?
qa.a: 'You don't know anything about art.'

qa.q: What does Ojas feel while writing this letter?
qa.a: Ojas feels sorry about the rude tone but still sure Kaka was wrong, and honestly wants to understand why the young cannot disagree.

qa.q: Why is Ojas's idea of a chai on the next visit a wise step?
qa.a: A private, calm talk lets Ojas disagree respectfully, so Kaka can hear the point without feeling shamed in front of the family.

qa.q: How might Swara feel about Ojas speaking up for her?
qa.a: Swara may feel grateful and supported, though perhaps uncomfortable that the dinner turned into a scene.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager honestly questioning why a younger person may not say an elder is wrong, and realising that a respectful private talk will be heard better than a public outburst.

passage:
"Amma, why couldn't I correct Thatha? He told the whole room the bridge was built in 1965. It was 1972. I checked."
Aparna kept drying plates. "You did correct him. In front of the Raghavans. With your phone held up."
"Because he was wrong!"
"He was. And you were right. But how did he look after that?"
Kalyani paused. "Quiet. He went to his room early."
"He felt small in front of his friends. Is that what you wanted?"
"No. I just... why can't younger people ever say an elder is wrong?"
"You can. Just not like a quiz show." Aparna smiled. "Take him his tea tomorrow. Tell him about 1972 alone. Ask how he remembers it."
Next morning Kalyani did. Thatha laughed. "Seventy-two! Yes, yes, I was mixing it up with my wedding year."

qa.q: When was the bridge actually built, according to Kalyani?
qa.a: It was 1972.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when asking why she couldn't correct Thatha?
qa.a: Kalyani felt frustrated and a little defensive, because she was right and couldn't see why that wasn't enough.

qa.q: What did Aparna suggest, and why did it work?
qa.a: Telling Thatha privately over tea and asking how he remembered it; without an audience he could laugh and admit the mix-up.

qa.q: How did Thatha feel after the public correction?
qa.a: Thatha felt small in front of his friends and went quietly to his room early.

grounding: Shows a teenager asking why an elder can't be corrected, and learning that the same point made privately and gently is heard better than a public correction.

passage:
I'm Pradeep, and on the drive to Mysuru last month I learned something the hard way.

Mama was driving, and he was sure the old highway was faster. The map on my phone said it was forty minutes slower. I told him. He said, "I've driven this road for twenty years." I said, louder, "Your twenty years are wrong, Mama!"

My cousin Tejas snorted. The car went silent. Mama took the old highway anyway, we were late, and nobody spoke till Srirangapatna.

I was right about the road. I was wrong about everything else.

On the way back, at a tea stop, I tried again, quietly, just the two of us. "Mama, can I show you something on the map? I might be wrong."

He looked for a long time. Then he clipped my phone into the dashboard holder. "Navigator," he said.

qa.q: How much slower did the map say the old highway was?
qa.a: The map said it was forty minutes slower.

qa.q: What does Pradeep feel now about the argument in the car?
qa.a: Pradeep feels embarrassed and regretful about the tone: right about the road, but wrong about everything else.

qa.q: Which choice worked on the way back, and why?
qa.a: Asking quietly, just the two of them, and leaving room to be wrong; Mama could listen without losing face in front of the family.

qa.q: What was it like for Mama when Tejas snorted?
qa.a: Mama likely felt embarrassed and challenged in front of the children, which made him dig in and take the old highway anyway.

grounding: Shows a teenager who publicly corrects an elder, sees it backfire, and finds that respectful private disagreement is heard.

passage:
Class teacher's note, 10B, Founders' Day — Mr Pradeep Rao

During today's talk, our guest, a retired alumnus in his eighties, said girls were not admitted to the school before 1970. Harsha stood up and said loudly, "That's wrong, sir. The 1958 photo in the corridor has six girls." A few students laughed. The guest lost his place and ended early.

Afterwards Harsha asked me, "Why is it rude when I'm right?"

A fair question. I said the facts were right; the stage and the tone turned it into a public correction of an old man in front of four hundred students.

What I did next: I suggested writing to him. Harsha wrote a polite note with a picture of the 1958 photo. His reply came today: "Thank you. I had forgotten my own classmates."

qa.q: How many girls are in the 1958 photo?
qa.a: The 1958 photo in the corridor has six girls.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when asking 'Why is it rude when I'm right?'
qa.a: Harsha felt confused and a bit stung, sure of the facts yet treated as rude for saying them.

qa.q: Why did the written note work better than the public correction?
qa.a: It kept the fact but removed the audience, so the guest could accept it with thanks instead of feeling shamed on stage.

qa.q: How might the guest have felt when the students laughed?
qa.a: The guest probably felt embarrassed and flustered, which is why he lost his place and ended early.

grounding: Shows a teenager honestly questioning why an elder can't be corrected, and a teacher guiding the same point into a private, respectful form that is heard.

passage:
Saturday night
Dinner at Nana's was a disaster. Chhote mama said at the table that the earth is closest to the sun in summer, which is why it's hot. It's NOT. We did this in class. So I said, "That's wrong, mama, it's the tilt." Everyone went quiet. Mummy gave me the look. Mama laughed but his ears were red. Later Mummy said I'd "insulted him in front of everyone". I said, "So I'm supposed to let him be wrong?" I cried in the bathroom, I don't even know why.
I called Parveen after. Her dadi is a retired professor. Parveen said her dadi says: correct in private, and start with a question. So after dessert I found mama on the balcony and said, "Mama, can I show you a diagram? I think the book says tilt." He looked. He said, "Hm. You're right, beta." Then he gave me his last ladoo.
Sangeeta

qa.q: What did Chhote mama say about summer?
qa.a: That the earth is closest to the sun in summer, which is why it's hot.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel after Mummy said she had insulted mama?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt hurt and frustrated, crying in the bathroom, because the question felt honest and fair.

qa.q: What made the second try work better?
qa.a: Correcting mama privately on the balcony and starting with a question let him hear the fact without losing face.

qa.q: How might Chhote mama have felt when corrected at the table?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed, laughing but with red ears, because he was corrected in front of everyone.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who asks why a younger person cannot correct a wrong elder, and learns that private, respectful disagreement is heard better.
